abstract:
<jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Purpose</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This article examines the strategic and ethical implications of regulatory arbitrage in global markets. While firms expand into less regulated environments to increase flexibility and growth, these strategies raise questions about long-term sustainability and corporate responsibility. The purpose is to show that regulatory arbitrage is not only a source of competitive advantage but also a potential source of strategic exposure, as actions taken in one market increasingly shape stakeholder perceptions across others.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Design/methodology/approach</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The article adopts a conceptual approach supported by a case-based illustration of the 2008 spin-off of Philip Morris International. Drawing on institutional and stakeholder perspectives, it develops a three-dimensional framework to analyze how regulatory distance, stakeholder visibility, and legitimacy spillover interact to shape the risks associated with global expansion strategies.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Findings</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The analysis shows that regulatory arbitrage can simultaneously generate economic value and increase legitimacy risk. While firms benefit from reduced constraints and expanded market access, these gains may be offset by heightened scrutiny and cross-market reputational effects. The findings suggest that strategic decisions cannot be evaluated solely within local regulatory contexts, as stakeholder expectations increasingly operate across global boundaries.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Originality/value</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This article introduces the concept of strategic exposure as a distinct extension of traditional views of regulatory arbitrage. The framework integrates institutional conditions with stakeholder evaluation to explain how global strategies produce both advantage and risk. It advances existing discussions through a clear emphasis on cross-market visibility and legitimacy spillover as defining features of contemporary global competition, offering a more precise way to assess the consequences of operating across uneven regulatory environments.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: The hidden risk of regulatory arbitrage: strategic exposure in global markets

abstract:
<jats:sec>
<jats:title content-type="abstract-subheading">Purpose</jats:title>
<jats:p>The global pandemic provides boards and executives an opportunity to evaluate if their organizations’ risk management systems were up to the challenge. Organizational risk management systems act like the body’s immune system, protecting the organization from threats. Most organizations struggled to deal with the crisis caused by global pandemic, with some failing to survive. This paper reviews the risk management steps and then examines at why some organizational risk management systems may have failed to protect their organizations from harm.</jats:p>
</jats:sec>
<jats:sec>
<jats:title content-type="abstract-subheading">Design/methodology/approach</jats:title>
<jats:p>This topic was inspired by discussions with executives and board members of organizations dealing with the pandemic. The paper was written based on their comments and was supplemented and contrasted with a review of risk management literature.</jats:p>
</jats:sec>
<jats:sec>
<jats:title content-type="abstract-subheading">Findings</jats:title>
<jats:p>The paper reviews what risk responses are effective in coping with the global pandemic and then discusses how a risk tool, the risk-value curve, can help boards and executive determine the optimal level of risk for their organizations going forward.</jats:p>
</jats:sec>
<jats:sec>
<jats:title content-type="abstract-subheading">Practical implications</jats:title>
<jats:p>Boards and executives can use the risk responses and risk tools reviewed to evaluate the quality of their risk management systems in light of the global pandemic.</jats:p>
</jats:sec>
<jats:sec>
<jats:title content-type="abstract-subheading">Originality/value</jats:title>
<jats:p>The paper is one of the first to critically examine why some organizational risk management systems failed and proposes risk management tools to help organizations deal with the next global crisis.</jats:p>
</jats:sec>
title: Revisiting risk management in a time of crisis

abstract:
<jats:sec>
<jats:title content-type="abstract-subheading">Purpose</jats:title>
<jats:p>The author offers executives a strategic process for proactively mitigating the risk of catastrophic unwanted Black Swan surprises that can severely, and often abruptly, impair a balance sheet.</jats:p>
</jats:sec>
<jats:sec>
<jats:title content-type="abstract-subheading">Design/methodology/approach</jats:title>
<jats:p>One practical way to apply the author’s approach is through hedging concentrated balance sheet exposures when market volatility is low or contracting.</jats:p>
</jats:sec>
<jats:sec>
<jats:title content-type="abstract-subheading">Findings</jats:title>
<jats:p>Though no one can reliably anticipate pandemics and related stock market turbulence, executives do not have to predict the future to economically protect their balance sheets from Black Swan events.</jats:p>
</jats:sec>
<jats:sec>
<jats:title content-type="abstract-subheading">Practical implications</jats:title>
<jats:p>Managers can construct Black Swan scenarios to assess how an unforeseen, disadvantageous future could develop and which risk management derivative would best mitigate it.</jats:p>
</jats:sec>
<jats:sec>
<jats:title content-type="abstract-subheading">Originality/value</jats:title>
<jats:p>This strategic approach to managing balance-sheet-threatening risks could help a firm outperform its competitors during future crises and catastrophes.</jats:p>
</jats:sec>
title: Risk as strategy: defending against catastrophic turns of fortune

abstract:
<jats:sec>
<jats:title content-type="abstract-subheading">Purpose</jats:title>
<jats:p>The increasing prevalence of enterprise risk coupled with global competition requires a strategic link to the way forward through measured outcomes determined in a collaborative and visual manner.</jats:p>
</jats:sec>
<jats:sec>
<jats:title content-type="abstract-subheading">Design/methodology/approach</jats:title>
<jats:p>The model was conceptualized and validated through strategic management deficiencies encountered in venture ownership, management consulting and teaching practice and was augmented with extensive stakeholder input and existing scholarly research.</jats:p>
</jats:sec>
<jats:sec>
<jats:title content-type="abstract-subheading">Findings</jats:title>
<jats:p>Managing risk is a complex and somewhat dark task that can happen everywhere or nowhere within a firm and requires mitigating strategies developed with stakeholder consensus. In practice with three distinct audiences of entrepreneurs, senior managers and capstone student strategists, the model does facilitate linked risk and opportunity identification as well as the quantification and/or qualification of variables. The process is as impactful as the outcomes when individual risk “appetites” and a collective risk culture emerge.</jats:p>
</jats:sec>
<jats:sec>
<jats:title content-type="abstract-subheading">Practical implications</jats:title>
<jats:p>Innovative organizations must regularly scan their external environment and assess internal resources and capabilities in a structured and actionable manner while understanding their risk culture. Valuable outcomes emerge from facilitating strategic risk management discussions, particularly in growing and informal organizations. Risk communications with stakeholders are complex and increasingly important.</jats:p>
</jats:sec>
<jats:sec>
<jats:title content-type="abstract-subheading">Originality/value</jats:title>
<jats:p>Opportunity mapping offers a novel process to identify prioritized strategies that may be otherwise determined intuitively with limited input or absent altogether. The process facilitates actionable outcomes as a supplement to the known practice of risk assessment while contributing to a competitive advantage.</jats:p>
</jats:sec>
title: Opportunity mapping: locating the upside of risk through visual mapping

abstract:
<jats:sec>
<jats:title content-type="abstract-subheading">Purpose</jats:title>
<jats:p>The purpose of the paper is to address customer alienation risk in the context of Marvel's recent (as of June 2023) under-performance and its contribution to Disney's stock's 50 percent-plus decline.</jats:p>
</jats:sec>
<jats:sec>
<jats:title content-type="abstract-subheading">Design/methodology/approach</jats:title>
<jats:p>Research followed recent developments at Disney/Marvel, as well as the Bud Light customer alienation, and reconciled those developments to core brand and strategic risk management resources to derive practical suggestions to mitigate customer alienation risk across industries.</jats:p>
</jats:sec>
<jats:sec>
<jats:title content-type="abstract-subheading">Findings</jats:title>
<jats:p>Marvel’s experience offers lessons that have relevance across industries inasmuch as a super hero paradigm is effectively a brand. The stronger the bond between customers and a brand, the more customers will maintain or extend their buying patterns over time. And the more customers personally identify with a brand, the greater the likelihood a customer alienation will occur if a firm disrespects that bond. Four practical suggestions are presented that will help to ensure the integrity of brands.</jats:p>
</jats:sec>
<jats:sec>
<jats:title content-type="abstract-subheading">Originality/value</jats:title>
<jats:p>While the under-performance of Disney/Marvel has been (and is) covered in the press, this is the first paper that we are aware of that links that under-performance to customer alienation risk.</jats:p>
</jats:sec>
title: Value destruction at Marvel, and how to manage customer alienation risk

abstract:
<jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Purpose</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This study examines how business owners (BOs) interpret institutional uncertainty and how such interpretations shape small and medium-sized enterprises’ (SMEs) financing behaviour. Focusing on Brexit in the United Kingdom, it investigates how sensemaking and behavioural mechanisms generate discouragement and self-rationing in accessing external finance.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Design/methodology/approach</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Adopting a constructive grounded theory approach, the study draws on twenty semi-structured interviews with UK SME owners conducted between December 2021 and January 2023. An abductive analysis was employed to develop a process-based explanation linking institutional uncertainty, entrepreneurial sensemaking, and financing behaviour.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Findings</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The findings show that institutional uncertainty does not simply constrain credit but reshapes entrepreneurial behaviour through interpretive and structural mechanisms. BOs translate uncertainty into heightened perceived risk, leading to precautionary sensemaking and consequent self-rationing even where credit remains available. Discouragement emerged as a multi-mechanistic process shaped by anticipated rejection, vicarious experiences, procedural burden, higher costs, imposter-related doubt, and perceived discrimination. Gender differences under uncertainty are not uniform in magnitude but mechanism-specific, with women experiencing stronger relational and identity-based barriers and men exhibiting more mindset-driven conservatism. Fintech-enabled lending mitigates discouragement by reducing relational and procedural barriers.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Originality/value</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This study extends discouragement theory by conceptualising it as an emergent and dynamic process of sensemaking under institutional uncertainty. It further integrates sensemaking and behavioural finance to offer a behavioural explanation for credit market disengagement. Additionally, it extends pecking order theory by identifying a behaviourally constructed pecking order, where sensemaking and self-rationing emerge endogenously through cognitive, social and identity-based mechanisms.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Discouragement under institutional uncertainty: entrepreneurial sensemaking and self-rationing in SME finance during crisis

abstract:
<jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Purpose</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This study proposes an integrative framework for hope leadership as an intersectional practice that bridges strategic and compassionate leadership. The framework integrates emotional, cognitive and critical hope as a conceptual model which engages an inclusive approach to strategy and compassion.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Design/methodology/approach</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>In response to the question posed as to what leadership models or frameworks best capture the intersection of these two approaches, this conceptual paper, uses Education as an illustrative example for the need to balance strategy and care through hope, with implications for future research and practice.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Findings</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This paper reframes the liminality between strategic leadership and compassionate leadership through an integrative framework for hope leadership as an intersectional practice of strategy and compassion.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Originality/value</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The study develops a new model for integrative hope leadership as a conceptually original contribution to considerations of strategy and compassion in leadership practice.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Hope leadership at the intersection of compassion and strategy: building an integrative framework to address volatility and uncertainty

abstract:
<jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Purpose</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This study examines how decision-makers interpret barriers in mergers and acquisitions (M&A) and how these perceptions shape strategic confidence in pre-acquisition decision-making under conditions of uncertainty.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Design/methodology/approach</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Drawing on survey data from 257 firms engaged in or considering M&A activity, the study employs a multi-stage quantitative approach. A Friedman test establishes a hierarchy of perceived barriers, while categorical regression with optimal scaling (CATREG) analyses the relationship between barrier recognition and three dimensions of strategic confidence: implementation capability, competitive advantage, and economies of scale.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Findings</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The results reveal a clear hierarchy of perceived barriers, with economic conditions, ineffective team integration, target valuation, and cultural differences emerging as the most salient challenges. Importantly, perceived barriers do not uniformly undermine confidence. Instead, they explain implementation-oriented confidence more strongly than strategic outcome confidence. Cultural differences are positively associated with confidence in execution, suggesting that awareness of complexity enhances perceived readiness, while ineffective team integration consistently erodes confidence across dimensions.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Practical implications</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>For practitioners, the findings suggest that effective M&A decision-making depends less on minimizing perceived barriers and more on systematically identifying and prioritizing them. Managers should interpret confidence not as certainty of success but as preparedness for execution, using barrier recognition as a tool for strategic alignment and integration planning.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Originality/value</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This study contributes to M&A research by shifting attention from post-acquisition outcomes to the role of perceived barriers in shaping strategic confidence during the pre-acquisition phase. Rather than conceptualizing barriers solely as obstacles, the findings suggest that their recognition may also support implementation readiness by functioning as diagnostic inputs for planning, coordination, and strategic alignment. In this way, the study offers a more nuanced perspective on how organizations prepare for M&A under conditions of uncertainty.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: From barriers to strategic readiness: how decision-makers build confidence in M&A under uncertainty

abstract:
<jats:sec>
<jats:title content-type="abstract-subheading">Purpose</jats:title>
<jats:p>To better understand the current state of world economic competitiveness as well as the challenges and opportunities both present and emerging for national economies, the IBM Institute for Business Value (IBV) 10;surveyed top executives on a range of topics related to their organizations’ and their nations’ successes.</jats:p>
</jats:sec>
<jats:sec>
<jats:title content-type="abstract-subheading">Design/methodology/approach</jats:title>
<jats:p>More than 2,700 C-level executives across the 12 largest national economies were surveyed in collaboration with Oxford Economics.</jats:p>
</jats:sec>
<jats:sec>
<jats:title content-type="abstract-subheading">Findings</jats:title>
<jats:p>•9;90 percent of executives cite skilled labor availability and quality as a critical factor for their organization when considering expansion into new markets. 10;•9;54 percent of executives say cyber threats are among the biggest strategic risks for their nation’s economy in the next five years. 10;•9;120 million workers in the world’s 12 largest economies may need to be retrained/reskilled in the next three years as a result of intelligent/AI-enabled automation. 10;</jats:p>
</jats:sec>
<jats:sec>
<jats:title content-type="abstract-subheading">Practical implications</jats:title>
<jats:p>By a wide margin, regulatory risk and cyber threats dominate the attention of business and other leaders as primary risks to their respective economies.</jats:p>
</jats:sec>
<jats:sec>
<jats:title content-type="abstract-subheading">Social implications</jats:title>
<jats:p>The future success of national economies is heavily dependent upon ecosystem partners working together to develop and maintain a skilled workforce across regional labor markets.</jats:p>
</jats:sec>
<jats:sec>
<jats:title content-type="abstract-subheading">Originality/value</jats:title>
<jats:p>Based on the responses, the researches recommend a focus on developing and maintaining the workforce skills required to realize value from intelligent automation and other emerging technologies.As intelligent automation and other disruptions continue to redefine industries, the types of skills these industries require are also evolving. 10;</jats:p>
</jats:sec>
title: Agility, skills and cybersecurity: critical drivers of competitiveness in times of economic uncertainty

abstract:
<jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Purpose</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This paper aims to explore how individual resilience contributes to organizational resilience through a processual perspective. While resilience is widely recognized as a multi-level construct, limited research has examined how personal experiences of individuals influence the resilience of organizations they lead.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Design/methodology/approach</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The study employs a qualitative analysis of secondary data, focusing on the life trajectory of Steve Jobs, widely regarded as a resilient individual who led a resilient organization. This biographical case study approach allows for the identification of individual and entrepreneurial resilience factors and traces how these factors are transferred and adapted at the organizational level.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Findings</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Our analysis suggests that resilience developed in personal life can be transferred to the entrepreneurial context and subsequently integrated into organizational dynamics. This transfer occurs through the adaptation and transposition of individual resilience behaviors into organizational practices. The study highlights the critical role of personal experiences in shaping durable organizational resilience.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Originality/value</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The paper contributes to resilience literature by proposing a dynamic approach that explicitly links individual and organizational resilience. It offers a conceptual framework demonstrating how personal and entrepreneurial resilience factors can be mobilized to enhance an organization’s adaptive capacity and performance. By bridging the gap between individual and organizational resilience, this research provides novel insights into the mechanisms through which personal resilience informs and strengthens organizational resilience.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Resilience in motion: tracing the path from individual to organizational resilience

abstract:
<jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Purpose</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This study investigates how the adoption of artificial intelligence (AI) in strategic processes contributes to organizational resilience. Specifically, it examines the mediating roles of organizational agility, innovation capability, and leadership competency in digital strategy in translating AI investments into sustainable resilience.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Design/methodology/approach</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>A quantitative research design was employed using a purposive sample of 328 managerial respondents from diverse industries. Data was collected through an online survey and analyzed using Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modeling (PLS-SEM) in SmartPLS 4. Validated multi-item Likert scales were applied to measure AI adoption, agility, innovation, digital leadership, and resilience.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Findings</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The results demonstrate that AI adoption has both direct and indirect effects on organizational resilience. While AI adoption directly enhances resilience, its impact is significantly amplified through the mediating mechanisms of agility, innovation, and digital leadership. Innovation capability emerged as the most potent mediator, underscoring the importance of AI-enabled innovation for long-term adaptability and resilience. Agility and digital leadership also played critical roles in enabling firms to withstand disruptions and sustain competitiveness in turbulent environments.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Research limitations/implications</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The study is limited by its cross-sectional design and reliance on self-reported data from a single regional context. Future research should employ longitudinal and cross-country comparative designs to assess the dynamics of AI adoption and resilience over time. Additional mediators, such as absorptive capacity and organizational culture, may further enrich the model.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Practical implications</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>For practitioners and policymakers, the findings underscore the need for AI adoption to be complemented by strategic capabilities that foster resilience. Executives should integrate AI with organizational structures that foster agility, innovation, and leadership development.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Originality/value</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This study provides empirical evidence demonstrating that AI alone does not yield resilience. Instead, resilience emerges when AI adoption is embedded within dynamic organizational capabilities and leadership competencies.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Artificial intelligence and organizational resilience: the mediating role of agility, innovation, and digital leadership

abstract:
<jats:sec>
<jats:title content-type="abstract-subheading">Purpose</jats:title>
<jats:p>As businesses in a wide range of industries increasingly adopt digital ecosystems, the benefits include opening up new and untapped customer segments and channels, enabling access to new and untapped talent pools and expanding previously unexplored modes of innovation. Ecosystems – defined as digitally enabled networks that enhance value propositions by linking business functions, suppliers, distributors, partners, customers and other stakeholders – are now an engine that drives performance. Multiple studies confirm that value creation and competitive advantage are increasingly tied to organizations’ ability to engage partners and stakeholders. IBM Institute of Business Value’s most recent research has found that revenue growth of ecosystem leaders outpaces others by a five-to-one ratio.</jats:p>
</jats:sec>
<jats:sec>
<jats:title content-type="abstract-subheading">Design/methodology/approach</jats:title>
<jats:p>Yet despite these notable successes there is also a dark side to digital ecosystem engagement. Large ecosystems have become a central to business strategy while little attention has been paid to the potential for cyber threats. Increased openness of business operations can result in greater risk.</jats:p>
</jats:sec>
<jats:sec>
<jats:title content-type="abstract-subheading">Findings</jats:title>
<jats:p>Security must graduate into a central enabler of business transformation. If businesses do not fundamentally rethink their security equation, ecosystems and the trust on which they are built, which often take years and billions of investment dollars to build, can be squandered in minutes by ever-growing security threats.</jats:p>
</jats:sec>
<jats:sec>
<jats:title content-type="abstract-subheading">Practical implications</jats:title>
<jats:p>Large ecosystems have become a central to business strategy while little attention has been paid to the potential for cyber threats.</jats:p>
</jats:sec>
<jats:sec>
<jats:title content-type="abstract-subheading">Originality/value</jats:title>
<jats:p>Mature, risk-mitigated ecosystems are starting to resemble a mature supply chain, where some risks are precluded by design, some partners are favored based on established trust criteria and remaining risks are explicitly managed transactionally as part of the partner relationship.</jats:p>
</jats:sec>
title: Building threat resilience into ecosystem strategy

abstract:
<jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Purpose</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>It is a critical challenge for leaders to encourage employees to cope with uncertainty and lead organizational change in times of volatility. Adaptive leadership enables managers to better cope with organizational change by leveraging followers’ personal resources. This study examines the relationship between adaptive leadership, employee resilience, hope, and change-related uncertainty, drawing on affective events theory and the broaden-and-build theory of positive emotions.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Design/methodology/approach</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>We collected responses from 382 Chinese employees via an online survey and analyzed them using Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modeling (PLS-SEM).</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Findings</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The result shows that adaptive leadership contributes to building hope and employee resilience while reducing change-related uncertainty. Moreover, mediation test results indicate that hope partially mediates the relationship between adaptive leadership and employee resilience.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Originality/value</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Bridging leadership theory and managerial practice, this paper offers insights by explaining how resilience can be built through adaptive leadership with the role of positive/negative emotion triggers, and contributes to actionable practices during organizational change.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Leading organizational change: building employee resilience through adaptive leadership

abstract:
<jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Purpose</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The purpose of this paper is to examine how hybrid leadership enhances employee adaptive performance in Sierra Leone’s resource-constrained banking sector, testing psychological empowerment and employee resilience as mediating mechanisms and digital transformation stress (DTS) as a hierarchical boundary condition.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Design/methodology/approach</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The study employed a cross-sectional survey design. Data were obtained from 303 employees across 8 commercial banks in Sierra Leone. Partial least squares structural equation modelling (PLS-SEM) was employed as the analytical tool to test the hypotheses of the study.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Findings</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Hybrid leadership was positively related to adaptive performance. Psychological empowerment partially mediated this relationship, while employee resilience did not. However, resilience positively influenced empowerment, suggesting a protective-enabling role. Digital transformation stress significantly moderated the effects of hybrid leadership on both empowerment and resilience, yet adaptive performance remained stable, indicating team-level buffering. Age – but not tenure – was a significant predictor of adaptive performance.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Practical implications</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Banking executives and HR professionals should train and appraise leaders who can integrate transactional and transformational behaviors contextually, operationalize empowerment through bounded autonomy and strengthen team-based adaptive supports such as cross-training, shared crisis protocols and peer coordination mechanisms to sustain performance under digital stress.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Originality/value</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This study extends Full-Range Leadership Theory to non-WEIRD, resource-constrained contexts by empirically validating configurational hybridity as a stress-responsive, resource-regulating practice. It clarifies that psychological empowerment functions as the primary motivational conduit while employee resilience serves a protective-enabling rather than direct performance-driving role. Critically, it identifies DTS as a hierarchical stressor ceiling that differentially impacts psychological and behavioral outcomes – a novel contribution to digitalization and occupational health scholarship.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: The empowerment–resilience pathway: how hybrid leadership drives adaptive performance in digitally stressed emerging markets

abstract:
<jats:sec>
<jats:title content-type="abstract-subheading">Purpose</jats:title>
<jats:p>The author addresses the looming question in the digital era: Can long-established firms adopt an existential mindset that enables them to survive and prosper?</jats:p>
</jats:sec>
<jats:sec>
<jats:title content-type="abstract-subheading">Design/methodology/approach</jats:title>
<jats:p>Disruptors take advantage of significant changes in the traditional value drivers in an existing market. The success of long-established companies often inhibits innovation, and most mature organizations struggle to excel.</jats:p>
</jats:sec>
<jats:sec>
<jats:title content-type="abstract-subheading">Findings</jats:title>
<jats:p>Greater reliance on controlled experiments can mitigate the failures of innovation based primarily on focus group research.</jats:p>
</jats:sec>
<jats:sec>
<jats:title content-type="abstract-subheading">Practical/implications</jats:title>
<jats:p>Competitors can be transformed into collaborators in many parts of the value chain, and alliances are outperforming the more conventional business development approaches.</jats:p>
</jats:sec>
<jats:sec>
<jats:title content-type="abstract-subheading">Originality/value</jats:title>
<jats:p>The author’s powerful message: Today’s leaders must adopt a new mindset in which bureaucracy is repudiated and responsiveness and adaptability are rewarded.</jats:p>
</jats:sec>
title: The existential mindset for corporate survival and growth: innovation and resilience

abstract:
<jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Purpose</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The rapid diffusion of artificial intelligence (AI) has intensified organizational efforts to enhance innovation, agility, and long-term resilience. However, many firms struggle to translate AI initiatives into sustained strategic outcomes. This study aims to examine how digital leadership, AI strategic orientation, and AI governance jointly shape digital capability and innovation, and how these capabilities foster organizational agility and strategic resilience.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Design/methodology/approach</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The study adopts a quantitative research design using survey data collected from 302 managers and professionals across organizations of varying sizes and sectors. Drawing on Dynamic Capabilities Theory and Upper Echelons Theory, the model is empirically tested using PLS-SEM to assess both measurement and structural relationships.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Findings</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The findings demonstrate that digital leadership and AI strategic orientation play central roles in building digital capability, whereas AI strategic orientation and AI governance significantly enhance innovation. Digital capability and innovation jointly foster organizational agility, which emerges as the key mechanism through which AI-related capabilities translate into strategic resilience.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Originality/value</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This study contributes to the literature by integrating AI strategic orientation and AI governance into a dynamic capability framework that explains strategic resilience. By empirically positioning organizational agility as the primary transmission mechanism between AI-enabled capabilities and resilience, the research offers a more nuanced understanding of how organizations can move beyond isolated AI initiatives toward sustained, capability-based transformation in turbulent environments.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: From artificial intelligence strategy to strategic resilience: the roles of digital leadership, AI governance, and organizational agility

abstract:
<jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Purpose</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This study aimed to examine the effect of digital leadership on organisational resilience within the higher education sector of an emerging economy. It further explored the mediating role of innovation culture in this relationship.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Design/methodology/approach</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Anchored on the Transformational Leadership Theory (TLT) and the Dynamic Capabilities Theory (DCT), the study adopted an explanatory sequential mixed method to first test the conceptual model quantitatively using PLS-SEM and subsequently provided rich contextual explanations through a qualitative study.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Findings</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The quantitative results established a significant influence of digital leadership on organisational resilience and a partial mediation of innovation culture in the baseline relationship. The qualitative analysis generated three themes that provided nuanced insights into the quantitative outcomes.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Practical implications</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The study offers practical insights for practitioners in management, leadership and strategy, particularly those in the higher educational setting. Issues like digital competency development, investment in digital technology infrastructure, modelling and supporting innovation, championing technology adoption and being agile and responsive to external changes are some of the key management and leadership strategies that this study has projected for higher education (HE) leaders.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Originality/value</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The study collected and analysed empirical data from participants in six universities in an emerging economy context to test a novel model involving digital leadership, organisational resilience and innovation culture. It contributes to theory by integrating TLT and DCT to explain the mechanisms through which digital leadership enhances institutional adaptability.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Leading through digital disruption: how digital leadership shapes innovation culture and organisational resilience

abstract:
<jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Purpose</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This paper examines how artificial intelligence (AI) disruption influences employee resilience, with particular attention to the heightened vulnerability of mid-career employees. It develops a five-proposition conceptual framework that positions perceived organizational support (POS) as the central mediating mechanism and ethical leadership and career stage as critical boundary conditions.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Design/methodology/approach</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Drawing on Social Exchange Theory (SET), the Job Demands–Resources (JD-R) model, and career development theory, the framework conceptualizes AI transformation as a macro-level demand that threatens not only skills but also professional identity and perceived value. POS is positioned as a core mediating resource, while ethical leadership and career stage (mid-career) operate as key boundary conditions shaping responses to AI-driven change.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Findings</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The model proposes that AI disruption undermines POS and, in turn, employee resilience. POS mediates this relationship, while ethical leadership strengthens its positive effects. Mid-career employees − who combine high expertise with heightened displacement anxiety − are identified as uniquely vulnerable compared with early- and late-career cohorts.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Research limitations/implications</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Future research should empirically test the framework through longitudinal and qualitative studies across industries and cultural contexts to examine resilience trajectories during AI adoption and the buffering role of leadership and organizational practices.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Practical implications</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The framework offers actionable guidance for leaders, organizations, and policymakers, emphasizing career-stage-sensitive reskilling, transparent AI communication, and ethical leadership practices. In service industries, these interventions help preserve mid-career talent and institutional knowledge, positioning resilience as a strategic capability rather than a peripheral HR concern.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Originality/value</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The study contributes by reconceptualizing resilience as socially co-produced, extending the JD-R model to treat AI as a compound demand, positioning career stage as a boundary condition in social exchange processes, and clarifying how ethical leadership enhances the credibility and impact of organizational support. It frames resilience not only as an HR issue but as a strategic capability essential for sustaining competitive advantage under AI-driven transformation.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Employee resilience under AI disruption: the mediating role of perceived organizational support & moderating effects of ethical leadership and career stage

abstract:
<jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Purpose</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This study investigates the influence of women leadership and ESG performance on corporate resilience, using firm value and EVA, in the context of pre-, mid-, and post-COVID-19 pandemic. It also examines significant differences in these variables across COVID-19 periods.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Design/methodology/approach</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Employing panel data analysis, the study examines 33 IDX KOMPAS100 companies from 2018-2023, resulting in 198 firm-year observations. Data were sourced from Refinitiv and Annual Reports.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Findings</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The study reveals that ESG performance does not significantly impact EVA or firm value. Women Leadership positively influence firm value but has no significant effect on EVA. Only changes in ESG performance are significant across the pandemic, whereas firm value shows significance only between pre- and post-COVID-19. No significant changes in EVA and female executive were observed.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Research limitations/implications</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The insignificant impact of ESG performance may stem from time lags in translating ESG efforts into financial outcomes.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Practical implications</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The study provides significant implications for research by extending the discussion on corporate resilience through the lens of gender diversity and ESG performance. The growing importance of ESG performance during the pandemic shows that companies have increased commitment on ESG efforts even during hardships.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Originality/value</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This study uniquely integrates female leadership and ESG performance to examine corporate resilience in Indonesia’s KOMPAS100 firms across COVID-19 phases, offering novel insights into gender diversity’s impact on firm value and challenging assumptions about ESG’s financial benefits in emerging markets.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Female leaders and ESG: corporate resilience in Indonesia’s KOMPAS100 across the COVID-19 phases

abstract:
<jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Purpose</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Anchored in Self-Determination Theory, this study examines whether and how female entrepreneurs leverage Fintech to build financial resilience and enhance their well-being. Specifically, it argues that autonomy, competence, and relatedness facilitated through Fintech usage strengthen financial resilience, which in turn improves overall well-being.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Design/methodology/approach</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The study adopts a quantitative research design based on cross-sectional survey data collected from 409 women entrepreneurs in Ghana. Ordinary Least Squares (OLS) regression was used as the primary estimation technique to test the hypothesized relationships. To account for the bounded nature of the dependent variable and strengthen robustness, Tobit regression was conducted as a supplementary analysis. In addition, conditional process analysis (PROCESS macro) was employed to further validate the mediating effect.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Findings</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The results show that Fintech usage significantly enhances financial resilience among female entrepreneurs, and financial resilience, in turn, positively influences their overall well-being. The findings confirm the mediating role of financial resilience in the Fintech–well-being relationship.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Research limitations/implications</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>By integrating Self-Determination Theory with inclusive Fintech research, this study contributes theoretically and empirically by demonstrating how access to inclusive financial resources influences entrepreneur well-being through financial resilience. However, the cross-sectional design limits causal inference.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Practical implications</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Fintech adoption represents an important policy lever for alleviating financial constraints faced by female entrepreneurs and improving their well-being. Policymakers should promote supportive measures such as enhancing digital infrastructure, improving interoperability, strengthening cybersecurity, and expanding digital literacy. Female entrepreneurs are also encouraged to deepen their engagement with mobile financial tools to better manage risk and enhance resilience.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Originality/value</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This study advances the literature by linking Self-Determination Theory with Fintech research to explain how financial inclusion fosters female empowerment and entrepreneur well-being through financial resilience. Drawing on evidence from women entrepreneurs in Ghana, it enriches scholarship at the intersection of gender, Fintech, and entrepreneurship.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Fintech-based inclusive financial resource and well-being of female entrepreneurs: the mediating role of financial resilience

abstract:
<jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Purpose</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This paper investigates how leaders of hybrid organizations can develop flexible mental models − or “agile minds” − to navigate digital strategy under uncertainty. The study introduces AI-assisted scenario thinking as a cognitive scaffold that reduces cognitive load and enhances leaders’ adaptive capacity.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Design/methodology/approach</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The paper adopts a conceptual, propositional theory development approach. Drawing on Cognitive Load Theory and the Human–AI Collaboration (HAIC) framework, it develops the “5F framework” (Foundation, Forces, Focus, Futures, Formations) and the corresponding five novel propositions, including an extended proposition. Each stage explains human–AI collaboration process in scenario thinking that allocates tasks between humans and AI according task complexity and levels of uncertainty (complementarity, substitution, symbiosis).</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Findings</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The paper integrates HAIC into scenario thinking process and theorizes five propositions showing how AI-assisted scenario thinking reduces extraneous and intrinsic cognitive loads while enhancing germane load for leaders and decision-makers. By shifting from rigid, means-end problem solving toward forward-working thinking, leaders can better revise schemas, recognize weak signals, and craft adaptive strategies under uncertainties in the digital age.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Practical implications</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The 5F framework provides managers with a structured method to leverage generative AI as a cognitive partner in scenario thinking. It clarifies when AI should complement, substitute, or co-evolve with human reasoning, offering a practical pathway to reduce mental overload while enhancing strategic agility.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Originality/value</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This study extends scenario thinking literature by offering a cognitive-process explanation of how AI-assisted foresight support strategic adaptability under certainty. Rather than proposing a new foresight method, this paper contributes a theoretically grounded framework that integrates Cognitive Load Theory and Human–AI Collaboration. This paper explains why and when scenario thinking can facilitate adaptive mental model development in digitally intensive organizational context.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: How AI-assisted scenario thinking develops “agile minds” for a successful digital strategy?

abstract:
<jats:sec>
<jats:title content-type="abstract-subheading">Purpose</jats:title>
<jats:p>Organizations face challenges in volatile, uncertain, complex and ambiguous (VUCA) environments. It is vital to manage the change’s rate and magnitude in new and different ways to stay competitive. This study focuses on the phenomenon of scenario planning that can help organizations proactively plan for, react and adapt to VUCA forces if and when they occur.</jats:p>
</jats:sec>
<jats:sec>
<jats:title content-type="abstract-subheading">Design/methodology/approach</jats:title>
<jats:p>Based on an extensive academic and practitioner literature review, we posit that corporate scenario planning involves eight different practical applications and associated benefits. These include risk identification, assessing uncertainty, organizational learning, options analysis, strategy validation and testing, complex decision-making, strategic nimbleness and innovation. We offer a novel typology and propose a more complete and holistic model of the scenario planning application and its intended outcomes. Mini-case studies from various sectors illustrate the process. The model demonstrates the relationship between different benefit-driven applications - inputs, process and output benefits – and identifies opportunities for further research.</jats:p>
</jats:sec>
<jats:sec>
<jats:title content-type="abstract-subheading">Findings</jats:title>
<jats:p>A previous typology study classified “what” and “why” related scenario planning research and literature. However, the why or associated benefits were not broken down at any level of detail, representing a gap in explaining the actual value of this management tool. The current study proposes a novel “why” focused typology of scenario planning benefits based on an extensive literature review. The novel typology adorned several benefits of scenario planning in an integrated model explained using systems theory. These benefits included risk, uncertainty, options analysis, strategic flexibility, complex decision-making, strategy testing and validation, innovation and organizational learning.</jats:p>
</jats:sec>
<jats:sec>
<jats:title content-type="abstract-subheading">Originality/value</jats:title>
<jats:p>First time in the literature, the relationship between input, process and output benefits of scenario planning is explained using systems theory. The novel typology proposed illustrates the practical applications of scenario planning in one complete model.</jats:p>
</jats:sec>
title: Strategic scenario planning in practice: eight critical applications and associated benefits

abstract:
<jats:sec>
<jats:title content-type="abstract-subheading">Purpose</jats:title>
<jats:p>An IBM survey of business, government and education leaders concluded that if left unresolved, an emerging global skills crisis will likely have profound effects on businesses and economies worldwide.</jats:p>
</jats:sec>
<jats:sec>
<jats:title content-type="abstract-subheading">Design/methodology/approach</jats:title>
<jats:p>To gauge current skills challenges and assess future needs, the IBM Institute for Business Value in cooperation with Oxford Economics surveyed more than 5,600 global executives representing 18 industries and 48 countries</jats:p>
</jats:sec>
<jats:sec>
<jats:title content-type="abstract-subheading">Findings</jats:title>
<jats:p>Fifty-five percent of all executives surveyed conclude that inadequate investment from private industry is the most important challenge to overcome in addressing skills development in the future.</jats:p>
</jats:sec>
<jats:sec>
<jats:title content-type="abstract-subheading">Practical implications</jats:title>
<jats:p>Personalized learning, powered by data-driven cognitive technologies, can enable personalized education – allowing individuals to readily take more responsibility over their skills future and improve outcomes for stakeholders across the business ecosystem.</jats:p>
</jats:sec>
<jats:sec>
<jats:title content-type="abstract-subheading">Originality/value</jats:title>
<jats:p>Sixty-nine percent of industry executives from outperforming companies…indicate their organizations are already collaborating with ecosystem partners to address skills-related issues, as opposed to less than half of lower performing businesses.</jats:p>
</jats:sec>
title: Responding to the global skills crisis

abstract:
<jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Purpose</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This study aims to study the phenomenon of Mid-Career Crisis (MCC) in the light of Self-Determination Theory (SDT), emphasizing the basic psychological needs of autonomy, competence, and relatedness. It introduces the concept of Neotenic Leadership (NL) as a leadership-driven approach to addressing these needs during the mid-career phase. The objective is to bridge theoretical insights with practical application by proposing an integrated framework that enables structured, actionable interventions.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Design/methodology/approach</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The methodology adopts an integrative review of literature to develop a conceptual framework grounded in established theories. The application of traits – Curiosity, Adaptability, Resilience, and Emotional Resonance (CARE), central to Neotenic Leadership – is illustrated through real-life vignettes in organizational settings, offering contextual evidence for applying NL strategies for addressing mid-career challenges.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Findings</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The research underscores the crucial role of Neotenic Leadership (NL) in fostering intrinsic motivation for mitigating mid-career crisis (MCC). By integrating NL with Self-Determination Theory (SDT), the study operationalizes NL through CARE framework, providing a structured and actionable approach for real-world application.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Research limitations/implications</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>While this study offers a strong theoretical foundation, empirical research is needed to validate the proposed framework and assess NL’s effectiveness in managing MCC. Further studies should also test the real-world impact on workplace engagement and intrinsic motivation.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Practical implications</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The study offers practitioner-oriented framework for leveraging NL to support transformative growth needed during MCC. By addressing the basic psychological needs (SDT), CARE-based leadership practices can help mid-career professionals rekindle a sense of control, curiosity and adaptability through interventions such as coaching, mentoring and targeted skilling programmes.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Originality/value</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The originality of the work lies in its two-fold contribution to theory and practice. It advances literature on leadership and career by integrating Neotenic Leadership (NL) with Self-Determination Theory (SDT) to mitigate mid-career crisis (MCC). To the best of the author’s knowledge, this is the first study to formally define NL and present it as a structured model, expanding the original conceptualization of neoteny in leadership (Bennis & Thomas, 2002). The research further offers implementable CARE traits that bridge theoretical insights with practical applications, illustrated through real-life vignettes.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Handle with care: mitigating mid-career crisis through neotenic leadership

abstract:
<jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Purpose</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This paper aims to quantify the effect of crisis events on corporate sustainability from the perspective of small and medium-sized enterprise owners and managers from European Visegrad region in key business sectors particularly in manufacturing, trade, and services.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Design/methodology/approach</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Utilizing structural equation modeling (SEM) on a sample of 725 SMEs across the Visegrad region, the authors identified sector-specific differences in how crisis events influence business sustainability perceptions. This study uses different statistical measures to analysis of the data and have found various interesting results.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Findings</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Findings reveal that the COVID-19 pandemic and the Russia-Ukraine war, while both impactful, had distinct effects on SME sustainability. Manufacturing SME leaders perceived the war as having a stronger adverse impact than COVID-19, whereas in the trade sector, only the pandemic significantly influenced sustainability. In the services sector, both crises were deemed crucial, with the pandemic perceived as the most impactful.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Research limitations/implications</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The implications of this study enhance crisis management and sustainability theories by illustrating how SMEs across sectors respond to distinct crisis events and adapt business models to maintain operations despite disruptions. These findings offer valuable insights for national institutions, enabling more targeted support for SMEs within key business sectors to strengthen resilience in the face of future crises. Since the study depends on survey data, and since the survey was conducted in four EU countries, the results suffer from external validity issues. This flaw has been considered as one of the limitations of this study.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Originality/value</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The originality of this study lies in incorporating the sectoral view, focusing especially on SMEs, and providing the owners’ and managers’ perspectives. Also, the study adds values toward existing literature particularly in the domain of small and medium enterprises.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: The effect of crisis events on sustainability of SMEs in Visegrad region of Europe: perspectives from leadership and strategy

               <jats:title content-type="abstract-heading">Design/methodology/approach</jats:title>
               <jats:p> – For an update the author asked the opinion of the world’s foremost authority, Harvard professor Clayton Christensen. </jats:p>
            </jats:sec>
            <jats:sec>
               <jats:title content-type="abstract-heading">Findings</jats:title>
               <jats:p> – According to Christensen, “We discovered that there are three types of innovations, only two of which we had caught in the [original] theory of disruption. </jats:p>
            </jats:sec>
            <jats:sec>
               <jats:title content-type="abstract-heading">Practical implications</jats:title>
               <jats:p> – The only permanent way out of the innovator’s dilemma is to change the game being played and adopt a new corporate focus in which innovation is a necessity, not an option. </jats:p>
            </jats:sec>
            <jats:sec>
               <jats:title content-type="abstract-heading">Originality/value</jats:title>
               <jats:p> – The article updates and broadens disruption theory. Disruption, as Christensen defines it, is a theory of competitive response.</jats:p>
            </jats:sec>
title: Christensen updates disruption theory

abstract:
<jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Purpose</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This paper aims to develop a practical, decision-oriented framework to help managers select an appropriate strategic response to disruptive innovation.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Design/methodology/approach</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This study adopts a conceptual approach grounded in the disruptive innovation literature. It synthesizes prior research to identify three key decision factors (urgency, internal capability and internal resistance) and integrates them into a structured decision framework supported by a decision tree. The framework is illustrated through two contrasting case analyses, followed by a cross-case comparison and a summary table, to show how different configurations of these factors are associated with different strategic responses.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Findings</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The analysis shows that effective disruption response depends on the alignment between strategy and context. External cooperation is most effective under high urgency and low internal capability, ambidexterity performs best when internal capability is high and resistance is low, and autonomous units are most suitable when internal resistance is high and urgency is low to moderate. Strategic misalignment increases the risk of delayed or unsuccessful responses.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Originality/value</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This paper offers a practical framework that links organizational conditions directly to strategic choice. It contributes by bringing together urgency, capability and resistance into a unified decision tool and by illustrating how different strategic responses may succeed or fail depending on their alignment with these conditions.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Navigating disruption: a practical framework for strategic response

abstract:
<jats:sec>
<jats:title content-type="abstract-subheading">Purpose</jats:title>
<jats:p>This Masterclass considers the lessons of two recent important books have contrasting but complementary insights to offer to company leaders and strategists on how to improve the odds for developing successful innovations in response to game changes in markets.”</jats:p>
</jats:sec>
<jats:sec>
<jats:title content-type="abstract-subheading">Design/methodology/approach</jats:title>
<jats:p>In Dual Transformation: How to Reposition Today’s Business While Creating the Future (2017), disruptive innovation experts, Scott Anthony, Clark Gilbert and Mark Johnson offer corporate leaders a “dual transformation” template for simultaneously repositioning the traditional core business in the face of disruptive change, while also creating new businesses to harness the growth potential typically unlocked by such disruption. In The Power of Little Ideas: A Low-Risk, High-Reward Approach to Innovation (2017), innovation guru, David Robertson, and his collaborator, Kent Lineback, offer companies a “third way” for coping with historic market inflections by innovating around a core product to make it more compelling, rather than having to choose between attempting the radical or incremental innovation of the product itself.</jats:p>
</jats:sec>
<jats:sec>
<jats:title content-type="abstract-subheading">Findings</jats:title>
<jats:p>The most powerful message that both books featured in this masterclass have to offer is that while it may be true, as they go on to observe, that large companies can’t innovate faster than the market, they can learn “to innovate better than the market,” through more imaginative use of legacy products, platforms and assets.</jats:p>
</jats:sec>
<jats:sec>
<jats:title content-type="abstract-subheading">Practical implications</jats:title>
<jats:p>A “third way” to cope with market disruption is based on innovating around the core product, by surrounding it with a set of complementary innovations, rather than re-featuring the product itself. All of the complementary innovations operate together with the product “as a system or family to satisfy a compelling promise to the customer.”</jats:p>
</jats:sec>
<jats:sec>
<jats:title content-type="abstract-subheading">Originality/value</jats:title>
<jats:p>Both Dual Transformation and The Power of Little Ideas, present different, but far from mutually exclusive, innovation strategies that can help many more great companies to survive disruptive competition.</jats:p>
</jats:sec>
title: Two strategies for innovating in the face of market disruption

abstract:
<jats:sec>
<jats:title content-type="abstract-subheading">Purpose</jats:title>
<jats:p>The masterclass describes how companies are rapidly moving away from firm-centric views of value to a more customer-centric perspective of how value is created and co-created in an age of ubiquitous connectivity and producer-consumer real-time interaction.</jats:p>
</jats:sec>
<jats:sec>
<jats:title content-type="abstract-subheading">Design/methodology/approach</jats:title>
<jats:p>This masterclass focuses on the insights of Harvard marketing expert Thales Teixeira’ book Unlocking the Customer Value Chain: How Decoupling Drives Consumer Disruption.</jats:p>
</jats:sec>
<jats:sec>
<jats:title content-type="abstract-subheading">Findings</jats:title>
<jats:p>Professor Teixeira argues that change in consumer behavior, rather than technology, is the primary source of disruption in many industries, particularly in those likely to be most impacted by digitization. By paying close attention to the customer’s value chain, entrepreneurs can spot potential new opportunities for disruption and incumbents can figure out how best to respond to potential challenges.</jats:p>
</jats:sec>
<jats:sec>
<jats:title content-type="abstract-subheading">Practical implications</jats:title>
<jats:p>When delving deeply into the customer value chain for disruptive innovation opportunities, it is important to recognize that customers always pay you with three ‘currencies,’ their money, their time and their effort.</jats:p>
</jats:sec>
<jats:sec>
<jats:title content-type="abstract-subheading">Originality/value</jats:title>
<jats:p>By highlighting the common phenomenon of decoupling and how it operates, Teixeira helps make its disruptive potential more transparent and predictable for both disruptors and incumbents alike. Teixeira’s research identified three different types of decoupling: value-creating decoupling, value-eroding decoupling and value-charging decoupling.</jats:p>
</jats:sec>
title: Decoupling: customer-centric perspectives on disruption and competitive advantage

abstract:
<jats:sec>
<jats:title content-type="abstract-subheading">Purpose</jats:title>
<jats:p>Under the co-direction of John Hagel, Deloitte’s Center for the Edge has been publishing important new studies of disruption with an ‘outcome-based approach to disruption.’ This research is discovering patterns that may help leaders institute defenses against threats and identify opportunities for innovators</jats:p>
</jats:sec>
<jats:sec>
<jats:title content-type="abstract-subheading">Design/methodology/approach</jats:title>
<jats:p>Deloitte research is focusing on patterns of disruption that hit more than one market, but not all markets. It is examining: what are the characteristics of markets that would make them vulnerable to a particular pattern?</jats:p>
</jats:sec>
<jats:sec>
<jats:title content-type="abstract-subheading">Findings</jats:title>
<jats:p>After six months of research, Deloitte has identified nine patterns that meet its outcome-based criteria. A number of the patterns are based on creating network effects that grow so quickly they become hard to compete with if the rival firm does not already have an established market position. Another set of the patterns identifies ways to fundamentally transform the value-cost equation, but without network effects.</jats:p>
</jats:sec>
<jats:sec>
<jats:title content-type="abstract-subheading">Research limitations/implications</jats:title>
<jats:p>More patterns may be discerned as the research proceeds.</jats:p>
</jats:sec>
<jats:sec>
<jats:title content-type="abstract-subheading">Practical implications</jats:title>
<jats:p>For example, if incumbents and innovators just think about driverless cars as the auto industry, they are never going to fully see the disruption that is coming. By contrast, by thinking about it as a mobility ecosystem, then many other key players, risks and opportunities become apparent</jats:p>
</jats:sec>
<jats:sec>
<jats:title content-type="abstract-subheading">Originality/value</jats:title>
<jats:p>The patterns identified by Deloitte research may provide leaders with insights into how to defend against specific disruptions and also offer innovators inspiration for new opportunities in established markets and Blue Ocean ventures.</jats:p>
</jats:sec>
title: Can new disruption research suggest defenses against threats and opportunities for innovators?

abstract:
<jats:sec>
<jats:title content-type="abstract-subheading">Purpose</jats:title>
<jats:p>Two recent books will be of considerable value to company leaders and strategists seeking to deepen their understanding of the major trends driving this current wave of global transformation: “No Ordinary Disruption: The Four Global Forces Breaking All the Trends” and “China’s Disruptors: How Alibaba, Xiaomi, Tencent and Other Companies are Changing the Rules of Business.”</jats:p>
</jats:sec>
<jats:sec>
<jats:title content-type="abstract-subheading">Design/methodology/approach</jats:title>
<jats:p>The author considers what dynamic capabilities that will be needed to compete in a world of “transient advantage,” like modern China, with its “complicated and quickly changing demand pattern,” hyper-competition, shifting industry boundaries, and “discontinuities in the regulatory context.” He believes that China is the business management laboratory within which these skills are already being honed.</jats:p>
</jats:sec>
<jats:sec>
<jats:title content-type="abstract-subheading">Findings</jats:title>
<jats:p>By the turn of the millennium, the total revenue generated by private [Chinese] companies had already risen to parity with those of the state-enterprise sector, and since then it has grown more than six times faster.</jats:p>
</jats:sec>
<jats:sec>
<jats:title content-type="abstract-subheading">Practical implications</jats:title>
<jats:p>The rise of China’s reform era entrepreneurs has come in three waves to date, each representing a significant progression in the collective capabilities and sophistication of the country’s ever-expanding entrepreneurial cadre.</jats:p>
</jats:sec>
<jats:sec>
<jats:title content-type="abstract-subheading">Originality/value</jats:title>
<jats:p>Foreign multi-nationals would be wise to consider “what capabilities will have to be developed in China, for China,” learn from their Chinese rivals and ask where it might be possible to use these new “China’ capabilities ” to enhance performance globally.</jats:p>
</jats:sec>
title: The next wave of global disruption and the role of China’s entrepreneurs

abstract:
<jats:sec><jats:title content-type="abstract-subheading">Purpose</jats:title><jats:p>The IBM Institute for Business Value, which has been conducting Global Chief Executive Officers studies for 15 years, has been reporting on CEO concerns about business and economic disruption and described their efforts to respond to it. But surprisingly, in the 2018 study CEOs also indicate that the shock of disruption is waning. Only 26 percent of the CEOs say new entrants are actually taking market share. 10; 10; 10;</jats:p>
</jats:sec>
<jats:sec><jats:title content-type="abstract-subheading">Design/methodology/approach</jats:title><jats:p>This report is based on input from 2,148 Chief Executive Officers (CEOs), who were interviewed as part of the 19th IBM Global C-suite Study. Both quantitative and qualitative responses were collected from 346 face-to-face meetings and 1,802 in-person phone interviews. To understand how top-performing organizations navigate disruption differently, IBM researchers applied cluster analysis to examine the approaches of three groups of CEOs – Reinventors,. Practitioners and Aspirationals. 10;</jats:p>
</jats:sec>
<jats:sec><jats:title content-type="abstract-subheading">Findings</jats:title><jats:p>Most CEOs see the emergence of platforms and the growing importance of network economics – both scale and scope – as the crucial drivers of future growth.</jats:p>
</jats:sec>
<jats:sec><jats:title content-type="abstract-subheading">Practical implications</jats:title><jats:p>Almost six in ten Reinventors co-create new products, services or experiences with their customers.</jats:p>
</jats:sec>
<jats:sec><jats:title content-type="abstract-subheading">Originality/value</jats:title><jats:p>Today’s CEOs have learned to not only accommodate but embrace disruption. Anticipating and responding to sudden and dramatic change has become standard operating procedure. Chief executives from top performing businesses understand that success requires collaboration with partners within ecosystems and on platforms. Indeed, Checklists for leaders are included.</jats:p>
</jats:sec>
title: Navigating disruption with ecosystems, partners and platforms
